Triggers.value: Specific body parts associated with the event
Night-time or waking up in the dark

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Going to sleep or lying in the dark

Memory.value: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

issues.item: Escape Route Planning: always plan an escape route before entering a place
issues.explanation: 'Always plan an escape route before entering a place' implies a persistent current external-danger / entrapment threat style that is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which centers on intrusive sensory memory linked to the child's illness (body parts, darkness, songs; reliving, fragments, present-tense memory). For trauma of a child's life-threatening illness, this strategy is clinically much less coherent than avoidance/sleep delay, and it is not supported by any Threat or Appraisal items. Given the formulation, Triggers and Memory are strongly linked, but this item reflects a different syndrome focus (situational escape/safety behavior) not represented elsewhere in the selected nodes.

vignette: Sang was a 42-year-old South Eastern Asian farmer living in a small rural community with his wife and two children. As he recounted the traumatic event of his youngest child's life-threatening illness, Sang's voice carried the weight of his profound grief and anxiety. It had been over a year since the incident, but Sang's mind often wandered back to those harrowing days when his son battled for his life in the hospital. The memory of the IV lines, the oxygen mask, and the beeping machines was seared into his consciousness. Any visual cue-a hospital bracelet, an ambulance siren-would trigger a flood of memories that felt as vivid as they were at the time. When Sang saw a nurse's uniform or heard a song that played on the radio during those tense hours, he found himself reliving the event in all its terrifying detail. Nighttime was particularly difficult for him. The darkness amplified his anxiety, and any sudden sound could send waves of fear through his body as if he were back at the hospital again. He often delayed sleep, staying up late into the night to avoid lying in the dark where memories might ambush him without warning. This habit had left Sang exhausted during the day, making it hard for him to focus on his farm work and leaving him feeling increasingly isolated. Sang's relationship with his wife had also suffered as a result of his condition. He found himself withdrawing from social interactions, both within and outside the family, to avoid triggering any distressing memories or feelings. This avoidance extended to conversations about the illness, which he tried to steer away from in hopes of maintaining some semblance of normalcy at home. One evening, Sang was out late working on the farm, unable to sleep due to the fear of reliving those terrifying moments again. He had come to believe that staying awake was his only defense against the intrusive memories and the constant feeling of threat they brought with them. His wife, sensing his distress but unsure how to approach him, felt increasingly disconnected from her husband. What frightened Sang most was the prospect of another medical emergency. The memory of those fragmented moments, appearing suddenly without warning and then disappearing just as quickly, left him on edge. He had come to believe that if he could control when and where he allowed himself to think about those events, he might be able to prevent them from overwhelming him completely. Despite his efforts to cope through avoidance and sleep delays, Sang's symptoms were starting to interfere with his daily life. His wife had finally suggested they seek help together after noticing the toll it was taking on both their relationship and his work. In therapy sessions, Sang expressed a deep hope that he could find ways to manage his triggers and avoidances without feeling like he needed to constantly guard against them. As he sat in his therapist's office for the first time, Sang felt a mix of fear and relief. He was afraid of what might come up during the sessions but also hopeful that with support, he could regain some semblance of peace and reconnect with his family without being haunted by the memories of that terrifying event.
